lessons.title: How data crosses a network
lessons.intro: Two programs on different machines talk by sending small pieces of data across a chain of devices. This module gives you the picture that the rest of the course fills in: packets, layers, and who starts a conversation.

steps.title: Client and server
steps.text:
A **server** is a program that waits for someone to contact it. A **client** is a program that starts the contact. The words describe roles in one conversation, not kinds of machine. Your laptop is a client when its browser loads a page, and a server when you run a development web server on it.

Every conversation in this course has the same outline:

1. The client finds the server's address.
2. The client opens a connection to that address.
3. The client sends a request.
4. The server sends a response.

When something fails, the first useful question is which of these four steps failed.

steps.title: Packets
steps.text:
A network does not carry a whole file or a whole web page in one piece. The sender cuts the data into **packets**, each a few hundred to about 1,500 bytes. Every packet carries the address it is going to and the address it came from, like an envelope.

Packets travel separately. Two packets from the same message can take different routes, arrive out of order, or not arrive at all. The network itself makes one promise only: it will try to deliver each packet. Putting the pieces back in order, and asking again for a missing one, is the job of software at the two ends.

steps.title: Hops
steps.text:
Between the client and the server sit **routers**. A router is a device that receives a packet, reads the destination address, and passes the packet to the next router that is closer to that address. Each pass from one device to the next is a **hop**.

A request to a server in another country often crosses 10 to 20 hops. No single router knows the full path. Each one only knows which neighbour to hand the packet to next.

steps.title: One lost packet
steps.text: A client sends a message that is cut into 28 packets. Packet 9 is dropped by an overloaded router on the way.

steps.title: Layers
steps.text:
Network software is built in **layers**. Each layer does one job and relies on the layer below it.

| Layer | Its job | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Application | What the two programs say to each other | HTTP, DNS |
| Transport | Deliver a stream of data to the right program | TCP, UDP |
| Network | Move one packet to the right machine | IP |
| Link | Move a packet across one cable or radio link | Ethernet, Wi-Fi |

The layers wrap each other. An HTTP request is placed inside a TCP segment, which is placed inside an IP packet, which is placed inside a Wi-Fi frame. The receiving side unwraps them in the opposite order.

You will see other layer lists with seven numbered layers (the OSI model). People still use two of its numbers in daily speech: "layer 4" means transport and "layer 7" means application.

steps.title: Why layers help you debug
steps.text:
Each layer can fail on its own, and each failure looks different. A cable that is unplugged is a link problem. A wrong address is a network problem. A program that is not running is a transport problem, because nothing accepts the connection. A page that returns an error is an application problem.

Work from the bottom up. If a lower layer is broken, nothing above it can work, so testing the upper layer first tells you little.

steps.title: Which layer
steps.text: A browser shows the message "404 Not Found" for one page on a site. Other pages on the same site load.

steps.title: Exercise: name the step
steps.text:
For each report, write which of the four steps from the first section failed: find the address, open a connection, send a request, or receive a response. Write one sentence of reasoning for each.

1. "The browser says the site's name could not be found."
2. "The page loads for 30 seconds and then says the connection timed out. The name is correct."
3. "The page loads at once and says 500 Internal Server Error."
4. "The download starts and stops halfway, every time."

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Find the address.** The name could not be turned into an address, so nothing was ever sent to the server.
2. **Open a connection.** The address was found, and nothing answered at it. No request could be sent yet.
3. **Receive a response.** The connection opened, the request arrived, and the server answered with an error of its own. The network did its job.
4. **Receive a response.** The request arrived and the response began. Something interrupts the stream of packets partway, such as a timeout on a device in the middle.

Reports 3 and 4 fail in the same step for different reasons. The later modules give you the tools to tell them apart.

questions.prompt: What does the network itself do about packet 9?

choices.text: It sends packet 9 again from the router that dropped it
choices.feedback: A router keeps no copy of a packet after it passes it on or drops it.

choices.text: Nothing. Software at the two ends has to notice and send it again
choices.feedback: The network only tries to deliver. Noticing a gap and resending is done by the endpoints, usually by TCP.

choices.text: It tells the sender to start the whole message again
choices.feedback: Nothing in the network tracks whole messages. Only single packets exist there.

questions.prompt: Which layer is the problem in?

choices.text: Link, because the page did not arrive
choices.feedback: A response did arrive. "404" is text the server sent back.

choices.text: Transport, because the connection failed
choices.feedback: The connection worked. The server received the request and answered it.

choices.text: Application, because the server answered and said the page does not exist
choices.feedback: Every lower layer did its job. The server's own program decided there is no such page.

lessons.title: IP addresses and subnets
lessons.intro: Every packet names the machine it is going to with an IP address. This module covers how to read an address, which addresses are private, and how a range of addresses is written.

steps.title: An IPv4 address
steps.text:
An **IPv4 address** is a 32-bit number. It is written as four numbers from 0 to 255 with dots between them, such as `203.0.113.10`. Each of the four numbers is one byte.

There are about 4.3 billion possible IPv4 addresses, which is fewer than the number of devices in use. Two things make up for that. Private addresses are reused inside every home and office, as this module shows. **IPv6** is a newer format with 128-bit addresses, written in hexadecimal groups such as `2001:db8::10`. Both are in use today, and the ideas in this course apply to both. The examples use IPv4 because it is shorter to read.

steps.title: A machine can have several addresses
steps.text:
An address belongs to a **network interface**, not to a machine. An interface is one connection to a network: a Wi-Fi card, a cable port, or a virtual one made by software. A laptop on Wi-Fi with a VPN running has at least three interfaces, each with its own address.

One interface exists on every machine. The **loopback** interface has the address `127.0.0.1` and the name `localhost`. A packet sent to it never leaves the machine. It is how a program talks to another program on the same machine.

steps.title: Private and public addresses
steps.text:
Three ranges of IPv4 addresses are reserved as **private**. Anyone may use them inside their own network, and routers on the public internet refuse to carry packets addressed to them.

| Range | Usual sight |
| --- | --- |
| `10.0.0.0` to `10.255.255.255` | Company and cloud networks |
| `172.16.0.0` to `172.31.255.255` | Cloud networks, container networks |
| `192.168.0.0` to `192.168.255.255` | Home routers |

Every other address is **public**: it is unique on the internet and reachable from anywhere, unless a firewall blocks it.

Since private addresses are reused everywhere, `192.168.1.23` in your home and `192.168.1.23` in a neighbour's home are different machines. A private address means something only inside its own network.

steps.title: Which one can be reached
steps.text: A colleague in another city sends you this: "My test server is running, open `http://192.168.0.14:8080`."

steps.title: Writing a range of addresses
steps.text:
A **subnet** is a block of addresses that share their first bits. It is written in **CIDR notation**: an address, a slash, and the number of leading bits that are fixed.

`10.0.1.0/24` means the first 24 bits are fixed and the last 8 are free. It covers `10.0.1.0` to `10.0.1.255`, which is 256 addresses.

A smaller number after the slash means a larger block, because fewer bits are fixed. Each bit you free doubles the size.

| CIDR | Fixed part | Addresses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `10.0.0.0/8` | `10.` | 16,777,216 |
| `10.0.0.0/16` | `10.0.` | 65,536 |
| `10.0.1.0/24` | `10.0.1.` | 256 |
| `10.0.1.16/28` | first 28 bits | 16 |
| `10.0.1.5/32` | all of it | 1 |

Two special forms are worth knowing by sight. `/32` is exactly one address. `0.0.0.0/0` fixes no bits, so it means every address there is.

steps.title: Is it in the range
steps.text: A firewall rule allows traffic from `10.0.4.0/22`. The fixed part is 22 bits, so the last 2 bits of the third number and all of the fourth are free. The third number can be 4, 5, 6 or 7.

steps.title: Where subnets are used
steps.text:
You will write CIDR ranges in three places.

- **Network layout.** A cloud network is given a large block such as `10.0.0.0/16` and cut into smaller subnets, for example one for web servers and one for databases.
- **Firewall rules.** A rule says which source range may reach a port.
- **Routing.** A route says which range is reached through which neighbour.

Two subnets that you connect must not overlap. If the office uses `10.0.0.0/16` and the cloud network also uses `10.0.0.0/16`, a machine cannot tell which side an address belongs to. Choose ranges with this in mind before the networks are joined, because changing them later means changing every machine's address.

steps.title: Exercise: plan the ranges
steps.text:
A team has the block `10.20.0.0/16` for a new system. It needs three subnets:

- web servers, up to 200 machines
- databases, up to 10 machines
- a management subnet for at most 5 machines

Write a CIDR range for each. Then answer: the company's office network is `10.20.0.0/16` as well. What will go wrong when the two are connected, and what would you change?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
| Subnet | Range | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web | `10.20.1.0/24` | 256 |
| Databases | `10.20.2.0/28` | 16 |
| Management | `10.20.3.0/28` | 16 |

A `/24` holds 256 addresses, which covers 200 machines. A `/28` holds 16, which covers 10 and 5. Cloud providers reserve a few addresses in each subnet for their own use, so a `/29` with 8 addresses would be too tight for 5 machines. Many teams would use a `/24` for all three, because private addresses cost nothing and a subnet that is too small is painful to grow.

The overlap is the real problem. With the same `/16` on both sides, an office machine sending to `10.20.1.15` cannot know whether that is a neighbour in the office or a web server in the cloud. The fix is to give the new system a block the office does not use, such as `10.21.0.0/16`, before anything is built in it.

choices.text: It goes to whatever has that address on your own network, or to nothing
choices.feedback: The address is private, so your router keeps the packet inside your own network.

choices.text: The internet routes it to the nearest machine with that address

The block ends at 10.0.7.255. The third number 8 is one past it.

lessons.title: Ports and sockets
lessons.intro: An IP address gets a packet to the right machine. A port gets it to the right program on that machine. This module covers what a port is, what "listening" means, and why a server can be running and still unreachable.

steps.title: What a port is
steps.text:
A machine runs many programs that use the network at once. Each one is told apart by a **port**: a number from 0 to 65535 that the transport layer adds to every packet.

An address and a port together name one endpoint, written with a colon: `203.0.113.10:443`.

Some port numbers have agreed uses, so that clients know where to look.

| Port | Usual use |
| --- | --- |
| 22 | SSH (remote terminal) |
| 53 | DNS |
| 80 | HTTP |
| 443 | HTTPS |
| 5432 | PostgreSQL |
| 6379 | Redis |

These are conventions. Nothing stops a web server from using port 8080, and development servers often do. Ports below 1024 are different in one way: on most systems a program needs administrator rights to use them.

steps.title: Listening
steps.text:
A server program asks the operating system for a port and waits. This is called **listening**. From then on, the system hands every new connection for that port to that program.

Only one program can listen on a given address and port at a time. If a second one tries, the system refuses, and you see an error such as "address already in use". The usual cause is an older copy of the same program that is still running.

When a packet arrives for a port that nobody listens on, the system answers with a refusal. The client sees "connection refused" almost at once. That quick refusal is useful: it proves the machine was reached and that the fault is the missing program, not the network.

steps.title: Which interface it listens on
steps.text:
A server listens on a port **and** on an address. The address decides which interface it accepts connections from.

- `127.0.0.1` means loopback only. Only programs on the same machine can connect.
- A specific address such as `10.0.1.5` means only connections that arrive at that interface.
- `0.0.0.0` means every interface the machine has.

This is the most common reason a server "works on my machine" and nowhere else. Many development servers listen on `127.0.0.1` by default, which is a safe default. To let another machine reach the server, it has to listen on `0.0.0.0` or on the right interface.

steps.title: Works locally only
steps.text: A developer starts an API on their laptop. Its log says `Listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000`. A teammate on the same office network opens `http://192.168.1.23:3000`, where `192.168.1.23` is the laptop's Wi-Fi address.

steps.title: The client's port
steps.text:
The client needs a port too, so that the response can find its way back to the right program. The client does not choose it. The operating system picks a free one from a high range, usually above 32768, for each new connection. This is an **ephemeral port**: it is used for that one connection and then released.

A connection is identified by four values together: the client address, the client port, the server address and the server port. That is why one browser can hold several connections to the same server at once. They differ in the client port.

steps.title: See what is listening
steps.text:
Every system has a command that lists the ports in use and the program that holds each one.


Read two columns first: the local address and the port. `127.0.0.1:3000` is reachable only from the same machine. `0.0.0.0:3000` or `*:3000` is reachable from other machines, if a firewall allows it.

steps.title: Refused or timed out
steps.text: A client tries to connect to `10.0.2.8:5432`. After 30 seconds it reports a timeout. On the server, the database is running and listening on `0.0.0.0:5432`.

steps.title: Exercise: read the listing
steps.text:
A server gives this listing:

```text
Local address      Program
127.0.0.1:5432     postgres
0.0.0.0:22         sshd
0.0.0.0:8080       api
10.0.1.5:9090      metrics
```

The machine has two interfaces: `10.0.1.5` on a private network and `203.0.113.40` on the public internet. For each of the four programs, write who can connect: the same machine only, the private network, or anyone on the internet. Then say which line you would change first, and why.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
| Program | Reachable from |
| --- | --- |
| `postgres` | The same machine only. |
| `sshd` | Both interfaces, so the private network and the internet. |
| `api` | Both interfaces, so the private network and the internet. |
| `metrics` | The private network only, since it listens on `10.0.1.5`. |

The database is set up well: only the API on the same machine can reach it.

The line to look at first is `sshd`. A remote terminal open to the whole internet is tried by automated scans all day. It is better limited by a firewall to a few source addresses, or bound to the private interface and reached through a VPN. Whether the API should be public depends on what it is for. If it is, it is normally placed behind a proxy on port 443, which a later module covers.

This paragraph is general guidance, not a statement of any organization's policy.

choices.text: A timeout after about 30 seconds
choices.feedback: A timeout means no answer at all. Here the laptop answers at once with a refusal.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The database is listening on the wrong interface
choices.feedback: `0.0.0.0` accepts every interface, and a wrong interface would give a quick refusal, not a timeout.

choices.text: Another program already uses port 5432
choices.feedback: Then the database would have failed to start with "address already in use".

choices.text: Something between the two machines drops the packets, such as a firewall
choices.feedback: No answer at all means the packets never reached the server, or the replies never came back.

lessons.title: Names and DNS
lessons.intro: People use names and packets need addresses. DNS turns one into the other. This module covers how a lookup works, what the common records mean, and why a DNS change does not take effect everywhere at once.

steps.title: What DNS does
steps.text:
**DNS** (the Domain Name System) is a worldwide lookup service. A client gives it a name such as `shop.example.com` and gets back an address such as `203.0.113.10`. This is called **resolving** the name.

Resolving happens before the connection opens. If it fails, nothing is ever sent to the server, and no server log will show the attempt.

A name is read from right to left. `com` is the top-level domain. `example.com` is a domain that someone registered under it. `shop.example.com` is a name inside that domain, chosen by its owner.

steps.title: How a lookup travels
steps.text:
Your machine does not ask the whole internet. It asks one **resolver**, usually run by your internet provider, your company or a public service. The resolver does the walking.

1. The resolver asks a **root server** where to find `com`.
2. It asks a `com` server where to find `example.com`.
3. It asks the **authoritative server** for `example.com`, which holds the real records, for `shop.example.com`.
4. It returns the answer to your machine and keeps a copy.

The authoritative server is the one place where the domain's owner edits records. Everything else is a copy.

steps.title: Records
steps.text:
A domain's data is a list of **records**. Each has a name, a type and a value.

| Type | Meaning | Example value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `A` | The IPv4 address of a name | `203.0.113.10` |
| `AAAA` | The IPv6 address of a name | `2001:db8::10` |
| `CNAME` | This name is an alias of another name | `shop.hosting.example.net` |
| `MX` | Where mail for the domain goes | `mail.example.com` |
| `TXT` | Free text, often used to prove ownership | `verify=abc123` |
| `NS` | Which servers are authoritative for the domain | `ns1.example.net` |

A `CNAME` adds a step. The client looks up the alias, gets another name, and looks that one up. It is how a service hosted by someone else is given a name in your domain: you point your name at theirs, and they are free to change the address behind it.

One name can have several `A` records. The client gets all of them and normally tries the first, which spreads clients across several servers in a simple way.

steps.title: Caching and TTL
steps.text:
Every record carries a **TTL** (time to live): the number of seconds a copy may be kept. A resolver that has a copy answers from it until the TTL runs out, without asking the authoritative server again. Your operating system and your browser keep copies as well.

Caching makes DNS fast. It also means a change is not seen everywhere at the same moment. After you change a record, each resolver keeps giving the old value until its own copy expires. For a TTL of 3600, some clients see the new address at once and others up to an hour later.

People call this "DNS propagation". Nothing is being pushed out. Old copies are expiring at different times.

steps.title: The change that did not arrive
steps.text: A record for `shop.example.com` has a TTL of 86400 (one day). At 09:00 the owner changes its address from the old server to a new one and switches the old server off at 09:05.

steps.title: Plan a change around the TTL
steps.text:
The safe way to move a name is to plan for the cache.

1. Days before, lower the TTL to something short, such as 60 seconds. Wait for the old TTL to pass, so every cached copy has the short one.
2. Make the change. Within about a minute, nearly every client has the new address.
3. Keep the old server running until its traffic has stopped.
4. Raise the TTL again.

A short TTL means more lookups and faster changes. A long TTL means fewer lookups and slow changes. Names that sit in front of things you may need to move quickly, such as a failover, are given short TTLs on purpose.

steps.title: Look a name up
steps.text:
Two commands ask DNS directly, which removes the browser and its cache from the picture.


In the answer, read the type, the value and the number before them, which is the TTL the resolver has left. Asking a second resolver is the quick way to see whether a change has reached some places and not others.

Two answers are easy to confuse. `NXDOMAIN` means the name does not exist. An empty answer with no error means the name exists and has no record of the type you asked for.

steps.title: Which failure
steps.text: A new service is given the name `reports.example.com`. From the office it resolves and loads. From a laptop at home, `dig reports.example.com` returns `NXDOMAIN`, while other names in `example.com` resolve.

steps.title: Exercise: move a site
steps.text: `www.example.com` has an `A` record with a TTL of 14400 (four hours) that points at an old server. You must move it to a new server on Thursday at 10:00 with as little failed traffic as possible. Write the steps with times. Say when the old server can be switched off, and how you would check your work before and after.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Wednesday, before 06:00.** Lower the TTL to 60. Copies taken before this moment last up to four hours, so by 10:00 on Wednesday every resolver holds a copy with the short TTL. Doing it a day early leaves room for error.
2. **Thursday, before 10:00.** Check that the new server answers correctly by sending requests straight to its address, without using the name.
3. **Thursday 10:00.** Change the `A` record to the new address. Check with `dig` against two different resolvers.
4. **Thursday 10:05 onwards.** Watch the old server's traffic. It should fall to almost nothing within a few minutes. Some clients ignore TTLs and keep an address for longer, so leave the old server running for a day or two.
5. **Later.** Switch the old server off, and raise the TTL back to a few hours.

The step people forget is the first. Lowering the TTL at the moment of the change does nothing for copies that are already cached with four hours left.

questions.prompt: What do visitors see during the rest of that day?

choices.text: All of them reach the new server from 09:00
choices.feedback: Resolvers that looked the name up earlier still hold the old address.

choices.text: Some reach the new server, and others fail until their resolver's copy expires
choices.feedback: Each cached copy lives for up to a day. Those clients are sent to a server that is now off.

choices.text: All of them fail until the next day
choices.feedback: A resolver with no copy, or an expired one, asks again and gets the new address.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The home resolver's copy has not expired yet
choices.feedback: An old copy of an existing record would give an old address, not "does not exist". A cached NXDOMAIN is possible, and it clears within minutes.

choices.text: The record exists only in a DNS server that the office uses
choices.feedback: Companies often run internal DNS for names that should resolve only inside their network. The public servers have no such record.

choices.text: The service is down
choices.feedback: DNS does not check whether the server is running. A record resolves the same either way.

lessons.title: TCP and UDP
lessons.intro: The network delivers single packets and may lose them. The transport layer turns that into something programs can use. This module covers the two transport protocols, what a TCP connection costs, and how one ends.

steps.title: What TCP adds
steps.text:
**TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) gives two programs a **connection**: a two-way stream of bytes that arrives complete and in order. To do that, it adds four things on top of plain packets.

- **Numbering.** Every byte has a sequence number, so the receiver can put packets back in order.
- **Acknowledgement.** The receiver reports which bytes arrived. The sender sends again whatever is not acknowledged in time.
- **Flow control.** The receiver says how much it can take, so a fast sender cannot flood a slow receiver.
- **Congestion control.** The sender slows down when packets are being lost, since loss usually means a router on the path is overloaded.

The program sees none of this. It writes bytes in at one end and reads the same bytes out at the other.

steps.title: Opening a connection
steps.text:
Before any data moves, the two sides exchange three small packets. This is the **three-way handshake**.

1. The client sends `SYN`: "I want to connect, and my numbering starts here."
2. The server answers `SYN-ACK`: "Accepted, and my numbering starts here."
3. The client sends `ACK`: "Received."

The cost is one **round trip**: the time for a packet to go to the server and for the answer to come back. On a path with 80 ms of round-trip time, every new connection waits 80 ms before the first byte of the request can be sent. This is one reason programs keep connections open and reuse them.

steps.title: What the three failures look like
steps.text:
The handshake fails in three different ways, and each tells you something different.

| What the client sees | What happened | Likely cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connection refused, at once | The machine answered with a reset (`RST`) | No program listens on that port |
| Timeout, after many seconds | No answer to the `SYN` at all | A firewall drops the packets, or the address is wrong or the machine is off |
| Connection reset, later | An open connection was cut with `RST` | The server program crashed, or a device in the middle closed an idle connection |

A refusal is quick because something replied. A timeout is slow because the client keeps sending `SYN` again and waiting, for 20 seconds or more by default.

steps.title: Loss inside a connection
steps.text: A client is downloading a file over TCP. One packet in the middle is lost. The packets after it arrive normally.

steps.title: Closing a connection
steps.text:
Each side closes its own direction by sending `FIN`, and the other side acknowledges it. A clean close therefore takes four packets, and one side can finish sending while it still receives.

A `RST` is the unclean way. It ends the connection at once and throws away anything not yet delivered. A program that reads from a connection the other side has reset gets an error such as "connection reset by peer".

Connections also end without either program choosing it. Firewalls, load balancers and home routers keep a table of open connections and drop entries that have been silent for too long, often after a few minutes. The two programs do not find out until one of them sends something. Long-lived connections avoid this by sending a small **keepalive** message at regular intervals.

steps.title: UDP
steps.text:
**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) adds almost nothing to plain packets. It adds ports, so a packet reaches the right program, and a checksum to detect damage. There is no handshake, no ordering, no resending and no connection.

A program sends a UDP packet and it may arrive once, never, twice or out of order. That sounds worse in every way, and for some uses it is better.

- **A lookup of one question and one answer.** DNS sends a query in one packet and gets the answer in one packet. A handshake would triple the work.
- **Live audio and video.** A packet that arrives late is useless. It is better to skip it than to pause the call while it is sent again.
- **Protocols that bring their own rules.** HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which is built on UDP and does its own ordering and resending.

| | TCP | UDP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setup | Handshake, one round trip | None |
| Delivery | Complete and in order | Best effort |
| Unit | A stream of bytes | Separate packets |
| Typical use | HTTP, databases, SSH | DNS, calls, games, QUIC |

steps.title: Which protocol
steps.text: A team builds a voice chat feature. Sound is cut into packets of 20 ms each. About 1 packet in 100 is lost on a typical mobile connection.

steps.title: Many short connections
steps.text:
Since each new TCP connection costs a round trip, and a secure one costs more, a program that opens a connection for every request pays that price every time. Two habits remove most of it.

- **Keep the connection open** and send the next request on it. HTTP does this by default.
- **Use a connection pool.** A program that talks to a database keeps a small set of open connections and lends one to each piece of work.

A pool has a limit. If every connection is lent out, the next piece of work waits. Under heavy load that wait can look like a network problem when no packet is being lost.

steps.title: Exercise: read the symptom
steps.text:
For each report, say whether the client was refused, timed out, or was reset, and name one likely cause.

1. A service reports "connect: connection refused" for `10.0.2.8:6379` the moment it starts.
2. A nightly job that runs one query every 30 minutes fails on its second query with "connection reset by peer". The first always works.
3. A new server in a different subnet cannot reach the database. Each attempt hangs for 30 seconds.

Then answer: which of the three would you expect to be fixed by restarting the client, and why is that not a real fix?

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Refused.** The machine at `10.0.2.8` answered, and nothing listens on port 6379. The cache server is not running, or it listens on `127.0.0.1` only.
2. **Reset.** The job keeps one connection open and is silent for 30 minutes. A firewall or the database itself drops idle connections sooner than that. The second query is sent on a connection that no longer exists.
3. **Timeout.** No answer to the `SYN`. A firewall rule does not allow the new subnet, or there is no route between the subnets.

Restarting helps only with the second. A fresh client opens a fresh connection, so the first query works again, and the fault returns 30 minutes later. The real fixes are a keepalive, a pool that checks a connection before lending it, or opening a new connection for each run of the job.

questions.prompt: What does the receiving program see?

choices.text: The file with a gap where the lost packet was
choices.feedback: TCP never hands data to the program with a hole in it.

choices.text: The later bytes first, and the missing ones when they arrive
choices.feedback: TCP delivers in order. Later bytes wait until the gap is filled.

choices.text: A short pause, then all the bytes in order
choices.feedback: TCP holds the later packets, waits for the lost one to be sent again, and then delivers everything in order.

questions.prompt: Why is UDP the usual choice here?

choices.text: UDP loses fewer packets than TCP
choices.feedback: Both run over the same network and lose the same packets. They differ in what happens next.

choices.text: Waiting for a lost packet would delay all the sound after it
choices.feedback: With TCP, 20 ms of lost sound would hold back everything behind it. Skipping 20 ms is barely heard.

choices.text: UDP packets are encrypted by default
choices.feedback: Neither protocol encrypts anything on its own.

lessons.title: HTTP on the wire
lessons.intro: HTTP is the application protocol behind websites and most APIs. This module looks at what is sent over the connection: the text of a request and a response, how connections are reused, and what the newer versions changed.

steps.title: A request
steps.text:
An HTTP request is a message with three parts.

1. A **request line**: the method, the path and the protocol version.
2. **Headers**: one `Name: value` pair per line, with extra information.
3. An optional **body**, after an empty line.

In HTTP/1.1 these are plain text lines sent over the TCP connection. The `Host` header is required. One address often serves many sites, and `Host` tells the server which one the request is for.

steps.title: A response
steps.text:
The response has the same shape. Its first line carries a **status code**, a three-digit number that says how the request went. The first digit gives the group.

| Group | Meaning | Common examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `2xx` | It worked | `200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content` |
| `3xx` | Look somewhere else | `301` moved for good, `304` not changed |
| `4xx` | The request was wrong | `400`, `401`, `403`, `404`, `429` |
| `5xx` | The server failed | `500`, `502`, `503`, `504` |

The split between `4xx` and `5xx` matters when you debug. A `4xx` says the client should change the request. A `5xx` says the request may have been fine and the fault is on the server side.

steps.title: How the receiver knows where a message ends
steps.text:
A TCP connection is a stream of bytes with no built-in message boundaries. HTTP has to say where each message stops, in one of two ways.

- `Content-Length: 44` gives the body's size in bytes. The receiver reads exactly that many.
- `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` sends the body in pieces, each with its own size in front, and a piece of size 0 at the end. It is used when the size is not known in advance, such as for a response that is produced as it is sent.

A wrong `Content-Length` breaks the connection in confusing ways. If it is too large, the receiver waits for bytes that never come. If it is too small, the leftover bytes are read as the start of the next message.

steps.title: Keeping the connection open
steps.text:
HTTP/1.1 keeps the TCP connection open after a response, so the next request skips the handshake. This is called **keep-alive**, and it is the default.

One limit remains. On a single HTTP/1.1 connection, requests are answered one at a time and in order. A slow response holds up every request waiting behind it. Browsers work around this by opening about six connections to each site.

steps.title: The slow first request
steps.text: A page needs 12 small files from one server over HTTP/1.1. The browser opens 6 connections. The first file on each connection is slow to produce, about 2 seconds, and the rest take 10 ms each.

steps.title: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
steps.text:
Both newer versions keep the same methods, paths, headers and status codes. What changed is how the messages are carried.

**HTTP/2** sends many requests and responses over one connection at the same time. Each belongs to a numbered **stream**, and their pieces are mixed on the wire. A slow response no longer holds up the others at the HTTP level. Headers are sent in a compressed binary form, not as text.

HTTP/2 still runs on TCP, and TCP delivers bytes in order. If one packet is lost, every stream waits until it is sent again, even streams whose data already arrived.

**HTTP/3** removes that wait by replacing TCP with **QUIC**, a protocol built on UDP. QUIC tracks each stream separately, so a lost packet delays only the stream it belonged to. It also combines the connection setup with the encryption setup, which saves a round trip.

| | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 | HTTP/3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Runs on | TCP | TCP | QUIC over UDP |
| Format | Text | Binary | Binary |
| Requests at once per connection | 1 | Many | Many |
| A lost packet delays | That connection | Every stream | One stream |

steps.title: Headers that change how the network behaves
steps.text:
Most headers are for the application. A few change what the network pieces in the middle do.

- `Host` selects the site on a shared address.
- `Connection: close` asks for the connection to be closed after this response.
- `Cache-Control` says whether a copy may be stored and for how long, by the browser and by caches in between.
- `Content-Encoding: gzip` says the body is compressed.
- `Retry-After` says how long to wait before asking again, on a `429` or `503`.

steps.title: Read a real exchange
steps.text: `curl` prints the request it sends and the response it gets. Lines that start with `>` were sent, and lines that start with `<` were received.

steps.title: Who is at fault
steps.text: A client sends a request and receives `502 Bad Gateway`. The site runs behind a proxy that passes requests on to an application server.

steps.title: Exercise: read the exchange
steps.text:
A client sends this request and waits for 60 seconds before it gives up.

```http
POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Host: files.example.com
Content-Type: text/plain
Content-Length: 500

(the client then sends 200 bytes and stops)
```

Explain why the server never answers. Then say what the client would see if the header had read `Content-Length: 100` and it had still sent 200 bytes on a connection that is kept open.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
The server was told to expect 500 bytes of body. It has read 200 and is waiting for the other 300 before it treats the request as complete. Nothing is wrong at the network level: the connection is open and idle. Each side is waiting for the other until a timeout ends it.

With `Content-Length: 100`, the server reads 100 bytes, treats the request as complete and answers it. The other 100 bytes stay in the stream. On a kept-open connection the server reads them as the start of a second request. They are not a valid request line, so the server answers `400 Bad Request` and usually closes the connection.

In both cases the fault is a length that does not match the body. The lesson for debugging is that a hang with no error is often one side waiting for bytes it was promised.

questions.prompt: When do the fast files start to arrive?

choices.text: At once, because they are small
choices.feedback: Each connection answers one request at a time. A fast file queued behind a slow one has to wait.

choices.text: After about 2 seconds, once the slow responses have finished
choices.feedback: All six connections are busy with a slow response. The other six requests wait behind them.

choices.text: Never, because the connections are closed after one response
choices.feedback: Keep-alive leaves them open. The requests are delayed, not dropped.

questions.prompt: What does the status say?

choices.text: The client sent a malformed request
choices.feedback: That would be a `4xx` code, such as `400`.

choices.text: The application returned an error page of its own
choices.feedback: An error the application produced itself would normally be a `500`.

choices.text: The proxy got no valid response from the server behind it
choices.feedback: `502` is written by the proxy. The application is down, crashed mid-response, or sent something the proxy could not read.

lessons.title: TLS and certificates
lessons.intro: Packets cross devices owned by many parties, and any of them can read or change plain data. TLS protects a connection against that. This module covers what TLS guarantees, how a certificate proves who the server is, and the errors you will meet.

steps.title: What TLS gives you
steps.text:
**TLS** (Transport Layer Security) runs between TCP and the application protocol. HTTPS is HTTP sent through TLS. It gives three guarantees.

- **Privacy.** The data is encrypted, so devices on the path see only that two addresses are talking, and how much.
- **Integrity.** If anything changes the data on the way, the receiver detects it and drops the connection.
- **Identity.** The client can check that the server really is the owner of the name it asked for.

The third is easy to overlook and matters as much as the first. Encryption alone would protect your data perfectly on its way to an impostor.

Some things stay visible. An observer still sees the server's address and port, the timing and size of the traffic, and normally the server's name, which the client sends unencrypted at the start so the server knows which site is wanted.

steps.title: Two kinds of key
steps.text:
TLS uses two kinds of encryption together.

- **Symmetric** encryption uses one shared key to both lock and unlock. It is fast, and it protects the actual data.
- **Asymmetric** encryption uses a pair: a **public key** that anyone may have and a **private key** that the owner never shares. What one of them does, only the other can check or undo.

The problem TLS solves at the start of every connection is this: the two sides have never met and must agree on a shared key while others may be listening. The key pair makes that possible. It is used briefly to prove identity and to agree on a fresh shared key. Everything after that uses the fast shared key.

steps.title: Certificates
steps.text:
A **certificate** is a signed document that says "this public key belongs to this name". It contains the names it is valid for, the public key, a start date and an end date, and the signature of whoever issued it.

The issuer is a **certificate authority** (CA): an organization that checks that the requester controls the name before it signs. Your operating system and browser ship with a list of CAs they trust, called **root certificates**.

Roots rarely sign server certificates directly. A root signs an **intermediate** certificate, and the intermediate signs the server's. This is a **chain**. The client follows it link by link until it reaches a root it already trusts.

steps.title: The handshake
steps.text:
After the TCP handshake, the TLS handshake runs. In TLS 1.3 it takes one round trip.

1. The client says which name it wants and which methods it supports, and sends its half of a key exchange.
2. The server answers with its half, its certificate chain, and a signature made with its private key.
3. The client checks the chain, the name, the dates and the signature. Both sides now compute the same shared key.

The signature is the proof of identity. Only the holder of the private key that matches the certificate could have made it.

steps.title: What the client checks
steps.text:
A certificate is accepted only if all four checks pass.

| Check | Fails when |
| --- | --- |
| Chain | No path leads to a trusted root, or the server did not send the intermediate |
| Name | The name the client asked for is not listed in the certificate |
| Dates | Today is before the start date or after the end date |
| Signature | The server cannot prove it holds the matching private key |

The name check uses the name in the URL, not the address. A certificate for `shop.example.com` does not cover `www.shop.example.com` or the bare address. A **wildcard** such as `*.example.com` covers one level: `shop.example.com` and not `a.shop.example.com`.

steps.title: Connecting by address
steps.text: A site at `https://shop.example.com` has a valid certificate. To skip DNS while testing, an engineer opens `https://203.0.113.10` instead, which is the same server.

steps.title: Expiry
steps.text:
Certificates expire on purpose. A short life limits the damage if a private key is stolen, and it forces the checks to be repeated. Public certificates last months, not years. The longest life that browsers accept has been shortened several times, and many certificates last 90 days or less.

An expired certificate is one of the most common causes of a sudden, complete failure. Every client refuses at the same second, and nothing in the application changed. Two habits prevent it: renew automatically, and alert well before the end date, for example at 21 days left, so a broken renewal is noticed in time.

steps.title: Where TLS ends
steps.text:
TLS protects one connection between two endpoints. In many systems the public connection ends at a load balancer or proxy, which decrypts the request and opens a second connection to the application. This is called **TLS termination**.

The second connection is a separate choice. It can be plain HTTP inside a private network, or TLS again. When someone says "the site uses HTTPS", it is worth asking which parts of the path that covers.

steps.title: Inspect a certificate
steps.text: Two tools show what a server presents. In the output, look for the names the certificate covers, its two dates, the list of certificates in the chain, and the line that reports the result of the checks.

steps.title: Works in the browser, fails in the job
steps.text: A site loads in every browser. A script on a server that calls the same URL fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate".

steps.title: Exercise: three reports
steps.text:
For each report, name which of the four checks failed and what you would do.

1. "At 02:00 every client started failing with a certificate error. Nothing was deployed."
2. "The new name `api.eu.example.com` gives a certificate error. The certificate is for `*.example.com`."
3. "A teammate fixed their script by turning certificate checking off."

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Dates.** The certificate expired at that moment. Renew it now. Then find out why the automatic renewal did not run, and add an alert that fires weeks before the end date.
2. **Name.** A wildcard covers one level. `api.eu.example.com` is two levels below `example.com`. Issue a certificate that lists that name, or one for `*.eu.example.com`.
3. **None was fixed.** Turning the check off removes the identity guarantee. The connection is still encrypted, to whoever answers. The script now accepts an impostor without complaint. Find the failing check and repair it. Most often the cause is a missing intermediate or a private CA that the machine does not have in its trusted list.

The third point is general guidance, not a statement of any organization's policy.

lessons.title: Routing, gateways and NAT
lessons.intro: A machine has to decide where to send each packet, and so does every router after it. This module covers how that decision is made, how private machines reach the internet, and why the reverse direction needs extra work.

steps.title: The first decision
steps.text:
When a machine sends a packet, it asks one question: is the destination in my own subnet?

- **Yes.** The packet is sent straight to that machine over the local link.
- **No.** The packet is sent to the **default gateway**, which is the router that connects this subnet to everything else.

A machine with the address `10.0.1.5` in the subnet `10.0.1.0/24` reaches `10.0.1.9` directly. For `203.0.113.10` it hands the packet to its gateway, often the first address in the subnet, such as `10.0.1.1`.

A machine with no gateway, or the wrong one, can talk to its neighbours and to nothing else. That exact symptom points here.

steps.title: Route tables
steps.text:
The rule above is a small **route table**: a list of destination ranges and where to send packets for each. Every machine and every router has one.

When several entries match a destination, the most specific one wins, which is the one with the longest prefix. `0.0.0.0/0` matches everything and is the least specific, so it acts as the default.

steps.title: Which route
steps.text: Using the route table above, a machine sends a packet to `10.0.200.4`.

steps.title: Both directions need a route
steps.text:
A connection needs packets to flow both ways. The request follows the routes on the way out, and the reply follows the routes of every device on the way back. Those are separate tables.

A common fault is a route in one direction only. The request arrives, the server answers, and the answer is sent somewhere else or dropped. From the client it looks like a timeout, and the server's log shows that the request came in. That pair of facts points at the return path.

steps.title: NAT: many machines behind one address
steps.text:
Private addresses cannot be used on the internet. **NAT** (network address translation) is how a private machine still reaches a public server.

The gateway has one public address. When a private machine sends a packet out, the gateway rewrites the source to its own public address and a port it chooses, and writes the mapping in a table. When the reply comes back to that port, the gateway looks up the table, rewrites the destination to the private machine, and passes it on.

The server on the other side never sees the private address. It sees one public address, shared by every machine behind that gateway.

steps.title: What NAT means in practice
steps.text:
- **Outbound just works.** A private machine can start connections to the internet.
- **Inbound does not.** A packet from outside arrives at the gateway with no table entry, and the gateway has no idea which private machine it is for. It is dropped. To accept inbound connections, the gateway needs a fixed rule, called **port forwarding**, or the machine needs a public address or a load balancer in front of it.
- **Everyone looks like one address.** A server sees all users behind one office as a single address. Limits and blocks that work per address affect all of them together.
- **Table entries expire.** A silent connection loses its entry after a few minutes, which is the idle cut described in the TCP module.

Cloud networks use the same idea. A subnet whose machines have only private addresses sends outbound traffic through a NAT gateway, and receives inbound traffic through a load balancer.

steps.title: Inbound through NAT
steps.text: A developer runs a web server on a laptop at home on port 8080. It listens on `0.0.0.0`. The home router's public address is `198.51.100.7`. A friend elsewhere opens `http://198.51.100.7:8080`.

steps.title: See the path
steps.text:
`traceroute` (`tracert` on Windows) shows the routers a packet passes. It sends packets that are allowed only 1 hop, then 2, then 3, and each router that discards one reports itself.


Read it with care. A row of `* * *` in the middle usually means that router does not reply to these probes, and it is still passing traffic. What matters is where the answers stop for good. If nothing answers after hop 2, look at what comes right after hop 2.

steps.title: Exercise: one direction only
steps.text:
A service in subnet A (`10.0.1.0/24`) calls a database in subnet B (`10.0.2.0/24`). Every call times out. You learn these facts:

- From the service, `traceroute` to the database reaches it.
- The database's log shows the incoming connection attempts.
- Subnet B's route table has two entries: `10.0.2.0/24 direct` and `0.0.0.0/0` to an internet gateway.

Explain what happens to the database's replies, and write the route that fixes it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
The outward path works: subnet A has a route to subnet B, the packets arrive, and the database logs them.

The database then answers to `10.0.1.5`. Subnet B looks that address up in its own table. It is not in `10.0.2.0/24`, so the only match is the default, and the reply is sent to the internet gateway. Internet routers drop packets for private addresses, so the reply is lost. The service keeps waiting and reports a timeout.

The fix is a route in subnet B for subnet A:

```text
10.0.1.0/24    send to the router that joins the two subnets
```

The method to remember is that a request seen in the server's log together with a timeout on the client means the return path is broken. Check the route table on the answering side.

questions.prompt: Where is the packet sent?

choices.text: Directly, because the address starts with `10.0.`

lessons.title: Firewalls and network rules
lessons.intro: A route decides where a packet can go. A firewall decides whether it is allowed to. This module covers how rules are written, why replies do not need their own rule, and how to lay out a network so that a mistake exposes less.

steps.title: What a firewall checks
steps.text:
A **firewall** looks at each packet and allows or drops it by comparing it with a list of rules. A basic rule uses facts from the packet's headers.

- the direction: **inbound** (arriving) or **outbound** (leaving)
- the protocol: TCP or UDP
- the destination port
- the source or destination address range

Firewalls sit in several places: on the machine itself, on the router at the edge of a network, and in cloud platforms as rules attached to a machine or a subnet. Cloud platforms call these security groups or network security groups. A packet may pass several of them, and every one must allow it.

steps.title: Deny by default
steps.text:
The last line in that table is the important one. A well-built firewall **denies by default**: anything that no rule allows is dropped. You then list what is needed and nothing more.

The opposite design, allowing everything and blocking known bad things, fails quietly. Every service that someone starts later is exposed until somebody remembers to block it.

A rule should be as narrow as the need. "TCP 5432 from the application subnet" is a good rule. "Any port from anywhere" is the absence of a firewall.

steps.title: Stateful rules
steps.text:
A connection has packets in both directions. You do not have to write a rule for the replies, because nearly all firewalls are **stateful**: they remember each connection that was allowed, and let its replies back through.

So the rule "allow inbound TCP 443" is enough for a web server. The responses leave without an outbound rule. In the same way, a machine with no inbound rules at all can still call out to other services and receive their answers.

Direction is always about who starts the connection, not about which way most of the data flows. A machine that downloads a large file from a server made an **outbound** connection.

steps.title: Which rule is needed
steps.text: An application server must call a payment service on the internet at port 443 and receive its answers. The server's firewall currently denies everything in both directions.

steps.title: Drop or reject
steps.text:
A firewall can refuse a packet in two ways.

- **Drop.** Discard it and say nothing. The client waits and eventually times out.
- **Reject.** Discard it and send back a refusal. The client fails at once.

Most firewalls facing the internet drop, so that a scan learns as little as possible. This is why a firewall problem usually shows up as a timeout, and a missing program as a quick refusal. It is the most useful single clue you have.

| Client sees | Usually means |
| --- | --- |
| Connection refused, at once | Reached the machine, nothing listens on the port |
| Timeout | A firewall dropped it, or there is no route |
| Works from one place, times out from another | A rule limited by source address |

steps.title: Layout: public and private subnets
steps.text:
Rules are easier to get right when the network is cut into zones.

- A **public subnet** holds the few things the internet must reach, usually only load balancers.
- A **private subnet** holds application servers. They have no public address. Only the load balancers may reach them.
- A further private subnet holds the databases. Only the application servers may reach it.

Each layer accepts traffic only from the layer in front of it. If one rule is wrong, there is still another layer behind it. This idea is called **defence in depth**.

steps.title: Rules by name, not by address
steps.text:
Addresses change as machines are replaced. Most platforms let a rule refer to a group of machines by name: "allow port 5432 from members of the `app` group". A new application server joins the group and is allowed at once. A machine that leaves the group loses access.

Prefer this to lists of addresses. A list of addresses is correct on the day it is written and slowly goes out of date, in both directions: new machines are blocked, and old addresses stay allowed after they are given to something else.

steps.title: The rule that is too wide
steps.text: To fix a connection problem quickly during an incident, someone adds this inbound rule to the database: "allow TCP 5432 from `0.0.0.0/0`". The database has only a private address.

steps.title: Exercise: write the rules
steps.text:
A system has a load balancer, two application servers on port 8080, a database on port 5432, and an admin subnet `10.0.9.0/24` whose machines may open SSH (port 22) to the application servers. The application servers call an external email service on port 443.

Write the inbound rules for each of the three layers and the outbound rule the application servers need. Use group names for sources where you can. Everything else is denied.

steps.title: One possible answer

| Protocol | Port | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TCP | 443 | `0.0.0.0/0` |

**Application servers, inbound**

| Protocol | Port | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TCP | 8080 | group `load-balancer` |
| TCP | 22 | `10.0.9.0/24` |

**Database, inbound**

| Protocol | Port | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TCP | 5432 | group `app` |

**Application servers, outbound**

| Protocol | Port | Destination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TCP | 5432 | group `database` |
| TCP | 443 | the email service, or `0.0.0.0/0` if its addresses are not fixed |

No rule is needed for replies, since the firewalls are stateful. Port 80 is left out on purpose. If the site should redirect plain HTTP to HTTPS, add TCP 80 from anywhere on the load balancer only.

These rules are an example for learning, and general guidance. They are not a statement of any organization's policy.

lessons.title: Proxies and reverse proxies
lessons.intro: Few requests travel straight from a client to the program that answers them. Something in the middle receives the request and sends it on. This module covers the two kinds of proxy, what a reverse proxy does for a server, and what gets lost on the way.

steps.title: Two kinds of proxy
steps.text:
A **proxy** is a program that accepts a request and makes a request of its own to someone else on the sender's behalf. Which side it works for gives it its name.

- A **forward proxy** works for clients. Machines inside a company send their outbound requests to it, and it fetches the pages for them. It can filter, log and cache what leaves the network. The server sees the proxy's address.
- A **reverse proxy** works for servers. Clients connect to it believing it is the site. It passes each request to one of the real servers behind it. The client never learns their addresses.

The rest of this module is about reverse proxies, since nearly every production system has one.

steps.title: Two connections, not one
steps.text:
A reverse proxy does not pass packets through. It ends the client's connection and opens a separate connection to the server behind it. The program behind a proxy is called the **upstream** or the **backend**.

This has consequences that surprise people.

- Each connection has its own timeouts, its own protocol version and its own TLS setup. The client may speak HTTP/2 to the proxy while the proxy speaks HTTP/1.1 to the backend.
- The backend sees a connection from the proxy's address, not from the client's.
- An error can be produced by either one. A `404` may come from the application. A `502` or `504` comes from the proxy.

steps.title: What a reverse proxy is used for
steps.text:
| Job | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| TLS termination | The certificate lives on the proxy. Backends receive plain HTTP. |
| Routing | `/api` goes to one group of servers and `/images` to another. One address serves many sites by `Host`. |
| Load balancing | Requests are spread across several copies of a backend. |
| Caching | A stored copy of a response is returned without asking the backend. |
| Compression | Responses are compressed before they are sent. |
| Protection | Oversized requests, floods and slow clients are stopped before they reach the application. |

Putting these jobs in one place means the application does not need to do them, and they are done the same way for every service.

steps.title: The lost client address
steps.text:
Since the backend sees the proxy as its client, the real client's address is gone unless the proxy passes it on. Proxies add headers for this.

- `X-Forwarded-For` holds the client's address. Each proxy on the path adds the address it received the request from, so the header can become a list.
- `X-Forwarded-Proto` holds `https` or `http`: the scheme the client used with the proxy.
- `X-Forwarded-Host` holds the original `Host`.

steps.title: Whose address is it
steps.text: An application limits each client address to 100 requests a minute. It reads the address from the TCP connection. It is then placed behind a reverse proxy with no other change.

steps.title: Trust only your own proxy
steps.text:
`X-Forwarded-For` is an ordinary header, and a client can send any value it likes. An application that believes the header from anyone lets a client claim to be any address.

The safe rule has two parts.

1. The outermost proxy that you control overwrites or appends to the header with the address it really saw.
2. The application reads the header only when the connection came from that proxy, and takes the entry that your own proxy wrote, which is the last one it added, not the first in the list.

The same care applies to `X-Forwarded-Proto`. An application that builds links or decides whether a request was secure must take that fact from its own proxy.

This is general guidance, not a statement of any organization's policy.

steps.title: The proxy's own errors
steps.text:
When the backend does not behave, the proxy answers the client itself.

| Status | The proxy is saying |
| --- | --- |
| `502 Bad Gateway` | I connected and got a broken answer, or the connection was refused or reset |
| `503 Service Unavailable` | I have no healthy backend to send this to |
| `504 Gateway Timeout` | I connected and waited, and no answer came before my time limit |

These codes are a gift when debugging. They say the client reached the proxy, so DNS, the public network and TLS all worked. The problem lies between the proxy and the backend, or in the backend.

A `504` often comes from mismatched time limits. If the proxy waits 30 seconds and a report takes 45 seconds to produce, the client gets a `504` while the application finishes the work and finds nobody to send it to.

steps.title: Which timeout
steps.text: A proxy has a 60 second limit for backend responses. The application has a 120 second limit for its own database queries. A slow query takes 90 seconds.

steps.title: Exercise: put a proxy in front
steps.text:
An application listens on `0.0.0.0:8080` with plain HTTP and is reached directly from the internet. It logs each client's address, redirects `http` to `https` by looking at the incoming request, and has a 5 minute limit for file uploads.

You place a reverse proxy in front that terminates TLS on port 443. List what breaks or changes in the application, and what you would set on the proxy and on the application for each point.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Logged addresses.** Every log line shows the proxy's address. Have the proxy set `X-Forwarded-For`, and have the application read it only for connections from the proxy.
2. **The redirect.** The application now receives plain HTTP for every request, so it redirects every request to `https`, which arrives again as plain HTTP. That is an endless loop. Have the proxy set `X-Forwarded-Proto` and base the redirect on it, or move the redirect to the proxy.
3. **Uploads.** The proxy has its own time limit and its own maximum body size, and both are usually far below 5 minutes and a large file. Raise them for the upload path, or uploads fail with `504` or `413`.
4. **Direct access.** Port 8080 is still open to the internet, so the proxy can be bypassed, and with it the TLS and any protection. Listen on a private interface, and allow port 8080 from the proxy only.

The fourth point is the one most often missed. A proxy protects only the traffic that has to pass through it.

choices.feedback: Every request now arrives from the proxy's address, so the application counts all users as one client.

choices.feedback: The proxy gave up first. The application was within its own limit and never learned that nobody was waiting.

choices.text: Both see a failure at 60 seconds
choices.feedback: The proxy closes its side. The application's query keeps running unless it notices and cancels.

lessons.title: Load balancers
lessons.intro: One server is a limit on how much work can be done and a single thing that can fail. A load balancer puts several servers behind one address. This module covers how it chooses a server, how it knows which servers work, and how to take one out without dropping requests.

steps.title: What a load balancer does
steps.text:
A **load balancer** receives traffic at one address and spreads it across a group of servers that all do the same job. The group is often called a **pool**, and its members are **backends** or **targets**.

It gives you two things.

- **Capacity.** Three servers handle about three times the traffic of one.
- **Availability.** When one server fails, the others keep answering, and clients need not notice.

Both depend on the servers being interchangeable. If a request can be answered correctly by only one particular server, the load balancer cannot help with it. That is the subject of the section on sessions below.

steps.title: Layer 4 and layer 7
steps.text:
Load balancers come in two kinds, named for the layer they work at.

A **layer 4** load balancer works with TCP connections. It chooses a server when a connection opens and passes every byte of that connection to the same server. It does not read the content, so it is fast and works for any protocol, including databases.

A **layer 7** load balancer understands HTTP. It reads each request and can choose a server per request, by path, by `Host` or by header. It can terminate TLS, add headers, retry a failed request and answer with its own error pages. It is a reverse proxy with a pool.

| | Layer 4 | Layer 7 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit it balances | Connections | Requests |
| Reads the request | No | Yes |
| Routes by path or host | No | Yes |
| Terminates TLS | Usually not | Usually |
| Works for non-HTTP traffic | Yes | No |

The difference matters with long-lived connections. One client that keeps a single connection open and sends a thousand requests on it puts all thousand on one server behind a layer 4 balancer.

steps.title: How a server is chosen
steps.text:
- **Round robin.** Each server in turn. Simple, and fair when requests cost about the same.
- **Least connections.** The server with the fewest requests in progress. Better when some requests are much slower than others, since a server stuck with slow ones gets fewer new ones.
- **Weighted.** A server with twice the weight gets twice the share. Used when machines differ in size, or to send a small share of traffic to a new version.
- **Hash.** A value from the request, such as the client address or a user ID, decides the server, so the same value always lands on the same one.

steps.title: Slow requests
steps.text: A pool of two servers uses round robin. One request in ten is a report that takes 30 seconds. The rest take 50 ms. By chance, several reports in a row land on server A.

steps.title: Health checks
steps.text:
A load balancer has to know which servers can take traffic. It asks each one at a fixed interval, for example every 10 seconds. This is a **health check**. A server that fails several checks in a row is taken out of the pool. When it passes several in a row, it is put back.

For HTTP, the check is a request to a path the application provides for this purpose, such as `/health`, and anything other than a `200` counts as a failure.

What that path does is a design decision.

- A check that only proves the process is running stays green while the application cannot reach its database.
- A check that tests every dependency turns every server red at once when one shared dependency has a brief problem, and the load balancer then has nowhere to send anything.

A good check answers one question: can **this** server do useful work now? It tests what is specific to this server, and it is cheap, because it runs many times a minute.

steps.title: Sessions and sticky routing
steps.text:
Suppose a server keeps a user's shopping cart in its own memory. The next request from that user may land on a different server, which has no cart. This is the main obstacle to load balancing.

There are two ways out.

- **Sticky sessions.** The load balancer sends each user to the same server every time, using a cookie or a hash of the address. It works, with costs: load becomes uneven, and when a server fails or is replaced, its users lose their state.
- **Stateless servers.** No server keeps anything between requests. The cart lives in a database or a shared cache that every server can reach. Any server can answer any request.

Stateless servers are the better design. Every later topic, from deploys to scaling, becomes easier when any server can be removed at any moment.

steps.title: Taking a server out
steps.text:
Removing a server while it is answering requests cuts those requests off. To avoid that, a load balancer **drains** it: it stops sending new requests and lets the ones in progress finish, up to a time limit. Only then is the server stopped.

The same applies when a server starts. It should receive traffic only after its health check passes, or the first users get errors from an application that is still loading.

A deploy that replaces servers one at a time relies on both: drain the old one, start the new one, wait for healthy, move on.

steps.title: The balancer can fail too
steps.text:
A single load balancer is itself a single point of failure. Managed cloud load balancers run as several copies across separate locations and hide that from you. If you run your own, you need at least two, with a way for one to take over the other's address.

Separate locations matter for the backends as well. Three servers in one data centre all stop when that data centre has a power failure. Spreading them across independent locations, which cloud providers call zones, means one such event removes a third of the capacity and not all of it.

steps.title: Which design
steps.text: A team deploys by stopping the old servers and starting new ones, one at a time, behind a load balancer. During every deploy a few users see `502` errors.

steps.title: Exercise: design the health check
steps.text:
An API needs a database for every request, and it calls an external address-lookup service for about 5% of requests. Three copies run behind a layer 7 load balancer.

Decide what `/health` should check. Say what happens with your design in each case: one server loses its database connections, the database itself is down, and the lookup service is down.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
`/health` checks that the process is running and that **this** server can reach the database, with a cheap query and a short time limit. It does not call the lookup service.

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| One server loses its database connections | Its check fails. It is taken out, the other two carry the traffic, and users see nothing. This is the case the check exists for. |
| The database is down | All three fail. The load balancer returns `503`. That is honest, since no server could answer anyway. Some balancers keep sending traffic when every target fails, which gives the same outcome. |
| The lookup service is down | The check stays green. 95% of requests work, and the 5% that need a lookup get a clear error from the application. |

Including the lookup service in the check would turn a partial failure into a complete one: every server would be taken out, and the 95% of requests that never needed it would fail too.

The rule is to check what makes this one server unable to work, and to leave shared, optional dependencies out.
