lessons.title: Timeouts, retries and backoff
lessons.intro: A network call can fail in a way a local call cannot: it can give no answer at all. This module covers how long to wait, when asking again is safe, and how well-meant retries can take a system down.

steps.title: Why a call needs a time limit
steps.text:
When a remote call gets no reply, the caller cannot tell which of these happened.

- The request never arrived.
- The request arrived and the server is still working on it.
- The server finished and the response was lost on the way back.

All three look the same from the caller's side: silence. The only tool against silence is a **timeout**: a limit after which the caller stops waiting and treats the call as failed.

Many libraries have no timeout by default, or one measured in minutes. A caller without a limit waits for as long as the other side stays silent. Each waiting call holds a thread, a connection and memory. One slow dependency can use up all of them, and then the caller cannot serve requests that have nothing to do with it.

steps.title: Two timeouts, not one
steps.text:
Set two limits for every call.

- A **connect timeout**: how long to wait for the connection to open. Inside one network a handshake takes a few milliseconds, so 1 to 3 seconds is generous. A longer wait rarely succeeds.
- A **read timeout** (or request timeout): how long to wait for the response once the request is sent. This depends on the work. A lookup may deserve 2 seconds and a report 60.

Choose the read timeout from measurements. If 99 out of 100 calls finish within 300 ms, a limit of 1 second lets normal calls through and cuts off the stuck ones. A limit of 30 seconds protects almost nothing.

steps.title: Timeouts along a chain
steps.text:
A request often passes through several services. Each has its own limit, and they must fit inside each other. An outer limit shorter than an inner one produces wasted work: the outer caller gives up, and the inner services keep working on a result nobody will read.

Give each layer less time than the layer in front of it. Better still, pass a **deadline** along with the request: the moment by which the whole request must be done. Each service checks how much time is left and stops when there is none.

steps.title: What the caller knows after a timeout
steps.text: A service sends "charge the card 40.00" to a payment provider. After 5 seconds with no response, it times out.

steps.title: When a retry is safe
steps.text:
Trying again fixes many failures, since most are brief. It is safe only if doing the operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. Such an operation is called **idempotent**.

| Operation | Safe to repeat? |
| --- | --- |
| Read a record | Yes |
| Set a value to 5 | Yes |
| Delete record 12 | Yes, the second time it is already gone |
| Add 5 to a value | No |
| Create an order | No, unless the request carries a key |
| Charge a card | No, unless the request carries a key |

An operation that is not idempotent can be made so with an **idempotency key**. The caller makes up a unique value for the operation and sends it with every attempt. The server remembers which keys it has completed and returns the stored result for a repeat without doing the work again.

Not every failure should be retried either. Retry a timeout, a refused connection, a `502`, `503` or `504`, and a `429` after the wait it names. Do not retry a `400`, `401`, `403` or `404`. The same request will fail the same way.

steps.title: How retries make an outage worse
steps.text:
Imagine a service that is slow because it is overloaded. Its callers time out and retry. Each original request is now two or three requests. The overloaded service receives more traffic at the moment it can handle the least, and recovers more slowly or not at all. This is a **retry storm**.

It multiplies through layers. If three layers each retry three times, one request from a user can become 27 requests at the bottom.

steps.title: Backoff, jitter and a budget
steps.text:
Three rules keep retries from doing harm.

- **Exponential backoff.** Wait before each retry, and double the wait each time: 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms. A struggling service gets room to recover.
- **Jitter.** Add a random amount to each wait. Without it, a thousand clients that failed at the same moment all retry at the same moment, again and again.
- **A limit.** Retry a small number of times, such as two or three. Also retry at one layer only, usually the one closest to the failure. A **retry budget** caps retries at a share of all traffic, for example 10%, so retries can never multiply the load.

steps.title: Stop calling what is down
steps.text:
When a dependency fails again and again, waiting for a timeout on every call is a waste. A **circuit breaker** watches the recent results. After enough failures it "opens": calls fail at once without being sent. After a pause it lets a few test calls through, and closes again if they succeed.

The caller gets a fast error it can handle, for example by showing the page without the optional part. The failing service gets no traffic while it recovers.

steps.title: The synchronized clients
steps.text: A cache server restarts. 5,000 clients lose their connections in the same second. Each retries after exactly 1 second, then 2, then 4.

steps.title: Exercise: set the limits
steps.text:
A web page calls a `profile` service, which calls a `recommendations` service, which queries a database. Measured times for normal calls: database 40 ms, recommendations 120 ms, profile 200 ms. Today no call has a timeout, every layer retries three times at once, and last week a slow database took the whole site down.

Choose a timeout for each layer, say which layer retries and how, and say what the page should do when recommendations are unavailable.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
| Call | Timeout | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| recommendations to database | 300 ms | Several times the normal 40 ms |
| profile to recommendations | 500 ms | Covers one database call plus the service's own work |
| page to profile | 1 s | The outer limit, longer than everything inside it |

**Retries.** Only one layer retries: recommendations retries its database read once, after a backoff of about 50 ms with jitter. That fits inside the 500 ms that its caller allows. The read is idempotent, so the retry is safe. The other layers do not retry. Before, one page view could become 27 database queries.

**Degrading.** Recommendations are optional. When the call fails or times out, the profile service returns the profile with an empty recommendation list, and the page is shown without that section. A circuit breaker on that call means that during an outage the page does not wait 500 ms every time.

Last week's outage needed all three faults: no time limits, retries at every layer, and an optional feature treated as required.

lessons.title: Latency and where time goes
lessons.intro: A request can be slow while every part of the system works. This module covers what network delay is made of, why round trips matter more than connection speed for most requests, and the standard ways to remove them.

steps.title: Latency and bandwidth
steps.text:
Two numbers describe a connection, and they are often confused.

- **Latency** is delay: how long one packet takes to arrive. It is measured in milliseconds. **Round-trip time** (RTT) is the time there and back.
- **Bandwidth** is capacity: how much data can pass each second. It is measured in megabits per second.

Think of what each one limits. A large download is limited by bandwidth. A small API call is limited by latency, because the data fits in a few packets and the time is spent waiting for them to travel.

Buying a faster connection raises bandwidth. It does nothing for latency, which comes mostly from distance.

steps.title: Where latency comes from
steps.text:
A signal in a cable travels at about two thirds of the speed of light, roughly 200 km per millisecond. Distance therefore sets a floor that no hardware can beat.

| Path | Typical round trip |
| --- | --- |
| Same data centre | under 1 ms |
| Same city | 1 to 5 ms |
| Across a continent | 40 to 80 ms |
| Between continents | 100 to 300 ms |
| Mobile network, added | 20 to 100 ms |

Routers, queues and wireless links add to this. The numbers vary, and the ordering holds. A call to a server on the other side of the world costs a few hundred milliseconds before any work is done.

steps.title: Count the round trips
steps.text:
For a small request, the total time is close to the number of round trips multiplied by the round-trip time. A first HTTPS request to a new server needs several.

1. DNS lookup: one round trip to the resolver, if the name is not cached.
2. TCP handshake: one round trip.
3. TLS handshake: one round trip with TLS 1.3.
4. The request and the response: one round trip, plus the server's work.

That is three round trips to the server before the first byte of the page arrives. At 100 ms each, the user waits over 300 ms when the server needs 5 ms to produce the answer.

steps.title: Which change helps
steps.text: An API call from a mobile app takes 400 ms. The server's own work takes 10 ms. The app opens a new HTTPS connection for every call. The round-trip time is 120 ms.

steps.title: Fewer round trips
steps.text:
Since round trips dominate, the main techniques all remove some.

- **Reuse connections.** Keep-alive and connection pools remove the handshakes from every call after the first.
- **Batch.** One request that asks for 50 records beats 50 requests for one record each.
- **Run calls in parallel.** Three independent calls of 100 ms take 100 ms side by side and 300 ms one after another.
- **Avoid chatty designs.** A loop that makes one database query per item is the most common cause of a slow page. Ten items cost ten round trips. It is called the N+1 problem: one query for the list, then one more for each of its N items.

steps.title: Move the data closer
steps.text:
When the round trips cannot be removed, shorten them.

- **A cache** keeps a copy of an answer near the place it is needed, so no trip is made at all. Browsers do this, and so do servers.
- **A CDN** (content delivery network) is a set of caches in many cities. A user is sent to the nearest one, which holds copies of images, scripts and other files that are the same for everyone. The TCP and TLS handshakes also happen with the nearby cache, so even uncached requests gain a little.
- **Regions.** Running the application in more than one part of the world puts the whole service nearer to users. It is the most work, since the data then has to be in several places as well.

steps.title: Size still matters sometimes
steps.text:
For large responses, bandwidth and size take over. Two points are worth knowing.

- **Compression.** Text such as JSON, HTML and scripts shrinks to a fraction of its size with gzip or a similar method. It costs a little processing and saves transfer time.
- **A new connection starts slowly.** TCP begins by sending only a few packets, about 14 KB, and raises the rate as acknowledgements arrive. A response that fits in that first group arrives in one round trip. A larger one needs more. This is called **slow start**, and it is one more reason reused connections are faster.

steps.title: Averages hide the slow cases
steps.text:
Latency is not one number. Most requests are fast and some are much slower, because of a lost packet, a busy server or a cold cache. An average hides those.

Use **percentiles**. The 50th percentile (p50) is the time that half of all requests beat. The p99 is the time that 99 out of 100 beat. If p50 is 80 ms and p99 is 2 seconds, one request in a hundred is very slow, and a user who makes 100 requests in a visit will probably meet one.

steps.title: The far-away database
steps.text: An application server is moved to a region close to its users. Its database stays in the old region, 80 ms away. A typical page runs 30 database queries, one after another.

steps.title: Exercise: find the time
steps.text:
A dashboard page takes 3.2 seconds for users in Asia. The server is in Europe, with a round-trip time of 250 ms. The browser makes 8 API calls for the page, one after another, each on a new connection. Each call takes 15 ms of server work. Responses are about 4 KB each.

Estimate where the 3.2 seconds go. Then list three changes in order of how much each saves, with a rough figure for each.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
Each call on a new connection costs a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake and the request: three round trips, or 750 ms, plus 15 ms of work. That would give 6 seconds for 8 calls, so the browser is already reusing some connections. With one new connection and 8 requests one after another, the estimate is 500 ms of handshakes plus 8 times 265 ms, which is about 2.6 seconds. Add DNS and the page itself, and 3.2 seconds is explained. Server work is 120 ms of it.

1. **Run the 8 calls in parallel**, or replace them with one call that returns everything. The requests then cost one round trip together, not eight. Saves about 1.8 seconds.
2. **Serve the API from a region in Asia**, or put a cache close to those users for the parts that are the same for everyone. Cuts each remaining round trip from 250 ms to perhaps 30 ms. Saves most of what is left.
3. **Make sure connections are reused** and HTTP/2 is on, so no call pays for a handshake twice. Saves up to 500 ms on later visits.

Speeding up the server's own code is last on the list. It accounts for less than 4% of the time.

choices.feedback: Later calls skip the TCP and TLS handshakes, which saves about 240 ms each time.

choices.text: It stays about the same
choices.feedback: The queries used to cost under 1 ms each inside one data centre.

choices.text: It gets much worse, by more than 2 seconds
choices.feedback: 30 queries at 80 ms each add 2.4 seconds. An application and its database belong close together.

lessons.title: Find where a request fails
lessons.intro: "It can't connect" describes a dozen different faults. This module gives you one order in which to test, the command for each step, and a table from error message to cause.

steps.title: Test in the order the request travels
steps.text:
A request goes through the same stages every time, and each stage depends on the ones before it.

1. **Name.** Does the name resolve, and to the address you expect?
2. **Path.** Can packets reach that address?
3. **Port.** Does something accept a connection on the port?
4. **TLS.** Does the secure handshake complete, with a valid certificate?
5. **HTTP.** Does the server answer, and with which status?
6. **Application.** Is the answer the right one?

Test them in this order and stop at the first that fails. Everything before it is proven to work, and everything after it cannot be judged yet. This turns a vague report into one narrow question.

steps.title: Step 1: the name
steps.text:
Check two things: that there is an answer, and that the address is the one you expect. An old address after a change points at a cached record. A private address where you expected a public one points at an internal DNS server giving a different answer inside the network.

Also check what the failing program uses. A container, a virtual machine and your laptop can each use a different resolver. Run the lookup from the place where the failure happens.

steps.title: Steps 2 and 3: the path and the port
steps.text:
One command tests both: try to open a TCP connection to the address and port.


There are three results, and each one means something different.

| Result | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Connected | The path and the port are fine. Move up. |
| Refused, at once | The machine was reached. Nothing listens on that port. |
| Timeout | No answer. A firewall drops the packets, there is no route, or the machine is off. |

`ping` tests the path alone, and it is less useful than it looks. Many networks block the packets that `ping` uses while they allow real traffic. A failed ping proves nothing. A successful TCP connection proves the path and the port.

steps.title: Refused from one place only
steps.text: From an application server, `nc -vz 10.0.2.8 5432` times out. From a second machine in the same subnet as the database, the same command connects.

steps.title: Steps 4 and 5: TLS and HTTP
steps.text:
`curl -v` shows both in one run. Read its output from the top.


Where the output stops is where the failure is. If it stops before "Connected", go back to steps 1 to 3. If it stops with a certificate error, it is step 4. If a status line appears, the whole network path works, and the status code tells you who is unhappy.

Two options help you separate causes.


The first reaches one particular server behind a load balancer and still sends the right name, so TLS and `Host` work. The second prints running totals over two lines, so the gap between two numbers is the time one stage took.

steps.title: From message to cause
steps.text:
| Message | Stage | Likely cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Could not resolve host, `NXDOMAIN` | Name | Typing error, missing record, wrong resolver |
| Connection refused | Port | Program not running, or listening on another address or port |
| Connection timed out | Path | Firewall, missing route, wrong address, machine off |
| No route to host | Path | No route from this machine to that network |
| Connection reset by peer | Port or later | Program crashed, or an idle connection was cut in the middle |
| Certificate has expired, name mismatch, unknown issuer | TLS | See the TLS module's four checks |
| `502`, `503`, `504` | HTTP | The proxy reached no working backend |
| `401`, `403` | HTTP | The network is fine. The credentials or permissions are not. |
| `404` | HTTP | The network is fine. Wrong path, or wrong site for this `Host`. |

steps.title: Compare two viewpoints
steps.text:
The most useful question in network debugging is: from where does it work, and from where does it fail? Run the same test from two places and compare.

- Works on the server itself, fails from another machine: the program listens on loopback, or a firewall on the machine blocks it.
- Works inside the network, fails from outside: an edge firewall, NAT, or a record that exists only in internal DNS.
- Works by address, fails by name: DNS.
- Works for one backend, fails for another: test each one directly with `--resolve`.

Each pair of results removes half of the system from suspicion.

steps.title: Change one thing at a time
steps.text:
When a test fails, change one thing and run the same test again. If you change a firewall rule, restart the service and edit DNS together, and it then works, you do not know which change mattered, and two of them may be wrong.

Write down what you tested and what you saw. In a long session it is easy to test the same thing twice, or to remember a result from before a change as if it were current.

steps.title: Where the time goes
steps.text: The timing command prints: `dns 0.004  connect 0.030  tls 0.058  first byte 2.960  total 2.961`.

steps.title: Exercise: walk the ladder
steps.text:
A colleague reports: "The new reporting service can't reach the billing API. It worked in testing." You are given these results, all run from the reporting service's machine.

```text
dig +short billing.internal.example.com      ->  10.0.3.14
nc -vz 10.0.3.14 443                         ->  succeeded
curl https://billing.internal.example.com/   ->  certificate verify failed:
                                                 unable to get local issuer
curl -k https://billing.internal.example.com/invoices  ->  HTTP 403
```

(`-k` tells curl to skip the certificate check.)

Say which stages are proven to work, where the first failure is, what probably causes it, and what the last line adds. Say what you would not do.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Proven.** The name resolves to a private address, so internal DNS works. A TCP connection to port 443 succeeds, so routes and firewalls allow the traffic and something listens there.

**First failure: TLS.** "Unable to get local issuer" is the chain check. The billing API's certificate is signed by a CA this machine does not trust. For an internal name, that is most likely the company's private CA, which was installed on the test machines and is missing from the new service's machine or container image. It could also be a missing intermediate.

**The last line.** With the check skipped, the request reaches the application and gets `403`. So there is a second, separate problem waiting behind the first: the reporting service's credentials are not allowed to read invoices. That is an application matter, and it would have stayed hidden until TLS was fixed.

**What not to do.** Do not leave `-k`, or its equivalent in code, in the service. Install the CA certificate so the check passes. Then fix the permission. They are two faults, to be fixed one at a time.

lessons.title: Trace and review a request path
lessons.intro: This module has no new ideas. You trace one request from end to end, review a network layout with faults in it, and plan one of your own. Do each exercise on paper before you read its answer.

steps.title: How to use this module
steps.text:
Each exercise has a step where you work alone and a step with one possible answer. The answers are not the only good ones. Compare your reasoning with them, and pay most attention to anything you did not think of at all.

When you review a layout, ask the same questions each time.

1. What can reach what, and should it?
2. Where does a single failure stop everything?
3. Where does a request wait, and for how long?
4. What would you see from the client if each part failed?

steps.title: Trace 1: one request, every step
steps.text:
A user in another country opens `https://shop.example.com/cart` for the first time today. The site has a CDN for images, a layer 7 load balancer that terminates TLS, three application servers in a private subnet, and a database.

Write every network step that happens before the cart appears, in order. Include each lookup, each handshake and each connection. For each step, name the protocol and say what would be seen if it failed.

steps.title: Count the round trips
steps.text: In trace 1 the user's round-trip time to the load balancer is 150 ms. Nothing is cached, and the browser uses TLS 1.3.

steps.title: Trace 1: one possible answer
steps.text:
| Step | Protocol | If it fails, the user sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Resolve `shop.example.com` | DNS over UDP | "Site can't be found" |
| 2. Route packets to `203.0.113.10` through the home router's NAT and many hops | IP | A timeout |
| 3. TCP handshake with the load balancer on port 443 | TCP | Refused or a timeout |
| 4. TLS handshake. The browser checks the chain, the name and the dates | TLS | A certificate warning |
| 5. Send `GET /cart` with `Host` and the session cookie | HTTP | - |
| 6. The load balancer picks a healthy server and sends the request to `10.0.1.6:8080` on a connection it keeps open, with `X-Forwarded-For` | HTTP over TCP | `502`, `503` or `504` |
| 7. The application takes a pooled connection and queries `10.0.2.8:5432` | TCP | `500`, or `504` if slow |
| 8. The response returns along the same two connections | HTTP | A partial page |
| 9. The browser resolves the CDN's name and fetches images from a nearby cache | DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP | Missing images |

Three things are easy to leave out. NAT at the user's end is part of the path. Steps 6 and 7 use connections that are already open, which is why they are cheap. Step 9 is a second, separate journey to a different server.

steps.title: Review 1: a network layout
steps.text: Read this description of a system and list every problem you find. Rank them by how urgent they are.

steps.title: The most urgent one
steps.text: Before you read the full list, choose from three of the faults.

steps.title: Review 1: what is wrong
steps.text:
**Exposure**

1. **The database is public.** It needs no public address at all. Put it in a private subnet and allow port 5432 from the web server only. A password is not a reason to skip the firewall.
2. **SSH is open to everyone.** Limit port 22 to an admin range or a VPN.
3. **Port 8080 is open.** It is probably the application behind a proxy on the same machine. If so, clients can bypass the proxy. Listen on loopback and close the port.
4. **`X-Forwarded-For` is trusted from anyone.** No proxy of the team's own writes it, so any client can claim any address.

**Availability**

5. **One web server.** Any failure or deploy is an outage. Use at least two behind a load balancer, in separate zones.
6. **A hand-renewed certificate.** One forgotten date takes the site down for every user at once. Renew automatically and alert weeks ahead.
7. **A one-day TTL.** If the server must be replaced in a hurry, some users are sent to the old address for a day. Use a few minutes, or point the name at a load balancer whose address does not change.

**Behaviour under failure**

8. **No timeout on the payment call.** If the payment API hangs, every request that calls it hangs, and the server runs out of capacity.
9. **Five immediate retries of a payment.** They multiply load on a struggling service, and a charge is not idempotent unless a key is sent. A customer could be charged several times.

Points 1 to 4 are general guidance on reducing exposure, not a statement of any organization's policy.

steps.title: Design: a small internal tool
steps.text:
Plan the network for an internal expenses tool. About 300 employees use it from the office network (`10.50.0.0/16`) and through a VPN. It has a web application, a database, and it sends email through an external provider. It must survive the loss of one server, and it must not be reachable from the internet.

Write down: the subnets and their ranges, what listens where, the firewall rules, the DNS record, where TLS ends, the health check, and the timeouts for the outbound email call.

steps.title: Design: one possible answer
steps.text:
**Subnets**, in a block that does not overlap the office: `10.60.0.0/16`.

| Subnet | Range | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Balancer | `10.60.1.0/24` | An internal load balancer, private address only |
| Application | `10.60.2.0/24` | Two application servers in separate zones |
| Data | `10.60.3.0/24` | The database, with a standby copy |

**Firewall rules**, with everything else denied.

| Target | Allow inbound |
| --- | --- |
| Load balancer | TCP 443 from `10.50.0.0/16` and the VPN range |
| Application | TCP 8080 from the load balancer |
| Database | TCP 5432 from the application group |

Outbound from the application: 5432 to the database, and 443 to the email provider through a NAT gateway. Nothing has a public address, so nothing can be reached from the internet.

**DNS.** `expenses.internal.example.com`, a record in internal DNS only, pointing at the load balancer, with a TTL of 300.

**TLS.** It ends at the load balancer, with a certificate from the company's CA that employee machines already trust. Renewal is automatic.

**Health check.** `GET /health` every 10 seconds. It checks the process and this server's database connection. It does not call the email provider.

**Email call.** Connect timeout 2 seconds, read timeout 10 seconds, at most two retries with backoff and jitter. Better: place the email on a queue, so that a slow provider never delays a user's request.

The survival requirement is met for the application by two servers and for the data by the standby. The decision that prevents the most trouble later is the first one: a block that does not overlap the office's.

steps.title: Where to go next
steps.text:
You can now follow a request through names, addresses, ports, connections, encryption, proxies and load balancers, and test each stage on its own.

Three habits are worth keeping.

- **Ask which stage failed** before asking why.
- **Compare two viewpoints.** Where it works and where it fails tells you more than either alone.
- **Give every call a time limit**, and decide what happens when it is reached.

The system design course builds on this one. It uses these parts, together with caches, queues and databases, to design whole systems and to reason about what happens to them under load and failure.

choices.feedback: Anyone can try passwords against it and attack flaws in the database software itself. A firewall rule that allows only the web server removes the exposure in minutes.

choices.text: The one-day TTL on the DNS record
choices.feedback: It makes moving the site slow. It does not expose anything.

choices.text: The missing load balancer
choices.feedback: It limits availability. It is a larger project and less urgent than an exposed database.
